stories.head: Spain's transport minister resigns after second deadly rail crash
stories.stand: Óscar Puente quit six days after a high-speed collision near Urda killed 69 people, saying no minister could stay after two such accidents in a year.
stories.say: Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente has quit, saying no minister could stay on after two crashes this serious in under a year. The collision near Urda killed 69 people.
body: Óscar Puente resigned as Spain's transport minister on Tuesday. A high-speed train collision near Urda, in Toledo province, had killed 69 people six days earlier.
He told a standing committee of parliament that no minister could stay on after two accidents this severe within a year. In January, a derailment on the same Madrid-Seville line killed 46 people.

According to Puente, a signalling system failed and controllers in Madrid let a Renfe train continue, although an Iryo train had stopped ahead. He announced extra safety measures, including more staff in control centres.
Puente is also withdrawing as a Socialist candidate for the 29 November general election. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez praised him for putting the victims first.

stories.head: Hoax bomb threats disrupt seven flights across Europe
stories.stand: Planes bound for Poland, Spain, Italy and Bulgaria were searched or diverted on Tuesday; no explosives were found and no group claimed responsibility.
stories.say: Seven flights across Europe were hit by bomb threats on Tuesday, forcing diversions and emergency landings in Poland, Spain and Italy. No explosives were found anywhere.
body: Seven passenger flights across Europe were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday, leading to searches, diversions and emergency landings. No explosives were found.

A LOT Polish Airlines jet from London Heathrow to Warsaw, with 181 people aboard, was diverted to Modlin airport. The airport closed temporarily while the plane was searched. An SAS flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw was also targeted.

Ryanair flights from Manchester to Murcia, from Lisbon and Dublin to Rome, and from Dublin to Sofia were affected. Italian Air Force jets escorted the Dublin flight into Rome. A Wizz Air flight from Bergamo to Sofia was also checked.

In Greece, the cruise ship Crown Iris, bound for Israel, was searched after a warning about explosives. A day earlier a Wizz Air flight from Luton was diverted to Budapest. No group has claimed responsibility.

stories.head: Death toll from Russian strike on Ukrainian aid centre passes 30
stories.stand: Rescuers are still searching for 48 missing people in Komyshuvakha as the US prepares to mediate talks between Ukraine and Russia next week.
stories.say: At least 31 people are now known to have died after Russian bombs hit an aid centre in Komyshuvakha, Ukrainian officials say, and 48 are still missing.
body: Ukraine's emergency service says at least 31 people died in a Russian air strike on a humanitarian aid point in Komyshuvakha. The village is in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Russian aircraft dropped aerial bombs on a school used to distribute aid on 2 November. Officials say 48 people remain missing. Two rescue workers and four police officers are among the dead.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strike showed that Russia did not want to de-escalate.
Separately, US envoy Steve Witkoff said Washington will mediate working-level talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi on 10 and 11 November.

stories.head: Greenland's parliament ratifies security deal with the United States
stories.stand: The agreement lets the US build two military bases on the island and bars countries outside the EU and NATO from strategic sectors.
stories.say: Greenland's parliament has approved a security deal with Washington that lets the US build two military bases, and keeps countries outside the EU and NATO out of strategic sectors.
body: Greenland's parliament, the Inatsisartut, ratified a security agreement with the United States on Tuesday. The vote was 16 in favour, with 7 abstentions and none against.
The deal allows the US to build two military bases on the island. It also bars countries outside the EU and NATO from strategic sectors, with the aim of limiting Chinese or Russian influence.

Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed it in New York in September. Denmark's parliament is expected to ratify it on 19 November.
Greenland is an autonomous Danish territory. Trump has repeatedly said the US needs to control it for strategic reasons, alarming Denmark.

stories.head: Trump says US will stop paying Israel's annual military aid
stories.stand: Trump said Washington would stop roughly $4bn a year in aid by the end of 2026, though a 2016 agreement runs until 2028.
stories.say: Donald Trump says the US will stop giving Israel about four billion dollars a year in aid by the end of this year, though the current deal runs until 2028.
body: Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the US would stop giving Israel about $4bn a year in aid. He spoke in a phone interview with Fox News as Americans voted in the midterm elections.
Trump said the payments would end by the end of this year, but gave no details of how. He said Israel no longer needed the money and that the US would keep selling it weapons.
The current agreement, signed in 2016, provides $3.8bn a year in military aid and runs until 2028. Annual funding still has to be approved by Congress.

Trump said Benjamin Netanyahu first proposed the idea. Netanyahu's office did not immediately comment. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot criticised the government for learning of the change through the media.

stories.head: Trump says no immediate plan for new US strikes on Iran
stories.stand: After a US strike on Qeshm Island, Trump said negotiations were delivering what Washington wants, while Qatar says hope remains for a deal.
stories.say: Donald Trump says the US has no immediate plans to strike Iran again after hitting Qeshm Island, and that indirect talks seem to be giving Washington what it wants.
body: Donald Trump told the Financial Times the US has no immediate plans to resume strikes on Iran, The Jerusalem Post reported. He said the US seemed to be getting what it wanted in indirect negotiations.
The remarks followed a US strike on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which a US official confirmed on Monday. Trump said the military remained ready if more strikes were needed.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman, Majed Al Ansari, said on Tuesday that hope remained for a deal. Qatar is working towards an interim agreement and passing proposals between the two sides.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday that the two countries were still far from a deal to end the war.

stories.head: North Korea fires missiles towards the sea as Americans vote
stories.stand: South Korea's military said projectiles were launched towards the East Sea on Wednesday morning, after a week of North Korean weapons tests.
stories.say: North Korea fired projectiles towards the East Sea on Wednesday morning, South Korea's military said, the latest in a run of weapons tests over the past week.
body: North Korea fired projectiles towards the East Sea on Wednesday morning, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said. The launch coincided with the US midterm elections.
According to SBS, the military said several missiles were launched from around Sondeok in South Hamgyong province. It was still analysing their type and range.
The launch followed a salvo of short-range missiles on 29 October and tests of cluster warheads reported by North Korean state media.
Kim Yo-jong, a senior official, said dialogue was one option for defending peace but not necessarily in the national interest.

stories.head: Indonesia detains three police generals over tapping of president's phone
stories.stand: Police say the generals ordered illegal taps on President Prabowo Subianto and other prominent figures in 2025 and 2026, then tried to delete the evidence.
stories.say: Indonesian police have detained three senior generals suspected of illegally tapping the phones of President Prabowo Subianto and dozens of other figures, then deleting the evidence.
body: Indonesian police have detained three senior police generals suspected of illegally tapping the phones of President Prabowo Subianto and other prominent figures.

Asep Safrudin, head of the police Criminal Investigation Agency, announced the detentions in Jakarta on Tuesday. Police say the targets included officials, politicians, journalists, activists and businesspeople, between 2025 and 2026.

Police allege the taps were ordered without proper procedure, and that the suspects later ordered recordings deleted to hide evidence. Investigators seized 11 mobile phones, an iPad and four flash drives.
Minister Yusril Ihza Mahendra said there was no indication of treason. The most serious charge carries up to 10 years in prison. No motive has been disclosed.

stories.head: Senegal's parliament rejects revised budget, clouding IMF deal
stories.stand: The vote threatens a planned $2.2bn IMF programme and deepens a feud between President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and assembly speaker Ousmane Sonko.
stories.say: Senegal's parliament has thrown out the government's revised budget, putting at risk a planned 2.2 billion dollar IMF programme as Ousmane Sonko feuds with President Faye.
body: Senegal's National Assembly rejected the government's revised 2026 budget on Tuesday, by 109 votes to 20 with three abstentions.

The vote could delay a three-year IMF programme worth about $2.2bn that Senegal is seeking to stabilise its finances. The IMF says public debt reached 132% of GDP at the end of 2024, after misreported borrowing under the previous government.
Ousmane Sonko's Pastef party controls the assembly, which he leads as speaker. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye dismissed Sonko as prime minister in May, and the two have been feuding since.
According to The Rio Times, the revised budget would have raised the 2026 deficit forecast to 7.6% of GDP. It is unclear whether the government will resubmit it.

stories.head: Explosion at Cameroon steel plant kills at least four
stories.stand: 16 people were seriously hurt in the blast and fire at the Metafrique Steel plant in Douala; the regional governor blamed safety failures.
stories.say: An explosion and fire at a steel plant in Douala, Cameroon, killed at least four people on Monday and left 16 seriously hurt, most with severe burns.
body: An explosion and fire at the Metafrique Steel plant in Douala, Cameroon, killed at least four people on Monday morning. The plant is in the Bassa industrial zone.
A further 16 people were seriously injured and taken to Douala General Hospital. Most have extensive burns and are in a critical condition.

Samuel Dieudonné Ivaha Diboua, governor of the Littoral region, criticised the company over safety measures imposed after a fire in May. He raised the possibility of suspending the plant's operations.
The cause of the explosion has not been established, and an investigation has been announced.

stories.head: Paraguay takes over Ueno Bank, cutting customers off from savings
stories.stand: The central bank says the lender's solvency fell below half the legal minimum; Ueno has about 3 million customers and past ties to President Santiago Peña.
stories.say: Paraguay's central bank has taken over Ueno Bank after its solvency fell below half the legal minimum. The digital lender says it has about 3 million customers.
body: Paraguay's central bank began a resolution procedure for Ueno Bank, one of the country's biggest lenders, on Tuesday. Its board had approved the step unanimously on Monday.

The central bank said Ueno's solvency ratio had fallen below half the legal minimum. Customers could not see balances, use the app or pay with cards on Tuesday. Ueno says it has about 3 million customers.
Deposits are guaranteed up to 228 million guaraníes, about $38,000, per depositor, to be repaid within 15 days. The state pension and health fund, IPS, has about $380m invested in the bank.
Central bank chief Carlos Carvallo ran Ueno before President Santiago Peña appointed him in 2023. Peña was a business partner of Ueno's owners until 2025. Peña and the bank deny wrongdoing.

stories.head: Learjet may have broken up before fatal Florida crash, NTSB says
stories.stand: All nine people aboard died when the jet, flying from Austin to the Bahamas, came down in Palm Beach County after the crew reported an overspeed.
stories.say: Investigators say a private jet that crashed in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine on board, may have been breaking up before impact. Weather is a major focus.
body: All nine people aboard a private Learjet 60 died when it crashed near Greenacres, in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday. The jet was flying from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.

The crew reported icing and moderate turbulence at 35,000 feet and asked to climb. Less than 30 seconds later the jet began descending fast, and the pilot declared an emergency, reporting an overspeed condition.
NTSB board member Tom Chapman said there was some indication the aircraft was breaking up before impact. Weather is a major focus of the investigation.
Technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson and members of his family were among the dead. A driver near the site suffered a leg injury, and residents of nearby mobile homes were evacuated.

stories.head: Lula and Sheinbaum skip Ibero-American summit in Madrid
stories.stand: Ten heads of state or government are due at the 30th summit, which opens on Wednesday; Argentina's Javier Milei attends despite a recent clash with Pedro Sánchez.
stories.say: Brazil's Lula and Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum are missing the Ibero-American summit opening in Madrid on Wednesday, while Argentina's Javier Milei attends despite a row with Pedro Sánchez.
body: The 30th Ibero-American Summit opens in Madrid on Wednesday without Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum. Venezuela's Delcy Rodríguez is also absent.
Heads of state or government from 10 countries are attending, including Spain, Argentina, Chile and Portugal. Colombia, Ecuador and El Salvador are sending vice presidents.
Argentina's President Javier Milei is attending although he called Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez a dictator during a visit two weeks ago. Chile's President José Antonio Kast is also present.
King Felipe VI opens the summit, and the plenary session is on Thursday. Planned agreements include a disaster-risk network, an artificial intelligence alliance and a charter on academic mobility.

stories.head: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor summoned to give evidence in fraud trial
stories.stand: Former banker Selman Turk, who denies dishonesty, won permission to call him as a witness in a case brought by Nebahat Isbilen.
stories.say: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been summoned to give evidence at a High Court fraud trial over money paid to him by a Turkish businesswoman. He is not accused of any wrongdoing.
body: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been issued with a witness summons to give evidence at a High Court fraud trial in London, the Daily Express reported on Tuesday.

Turkish businesswoman Nebahat Isbilen is suing her former adviser, ex-Goldman Sachs banker Selman Turk. She alleges he misled her over a £750,000 payment made to Andrew in 2019, which was later repaid. Her lawyers say tens of millions of her funds were misappropriated. Mr Turk denies dishonesty.
On 23 October Mr Justice Adam Johnson ruled that Mr Turk could seek evidence from Andrew. The judge said a summons would likely be needed because Andrew would probably not give evidence voluntarily.
Andrew is not accused of wrongdoing. The trial is expected to last 11 weeks.

stories.head: King calls slave trade a shameful chapter but stops short of apology
stories.stand: Andy Burnham has said he is open to a formal apology but rules out reparations; the palace says policy change is not for the King.
stories.say: Opening the Commonwealth summit in Antigua on Tuesday, the King said the transatlantic slave trade filled him with horror and profound sorrow, but he did not apologise.
body: King Charles opened the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in St John's, Antigua, on Tuesday. He called the transatlantic slave trade a shameful chapter of history that still casts a shadow over Commonwealth members.
He said it filled him with horror and the most profound personal sorrow. He did not offer an apology, and noted the Royal Navy's role in ending the trade.

A palace spokesperson said it would not be appropriate for the King to announce a change in government policy. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he is open to a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations.
St Lucia's Prime Minister Philip J Pierre, who chairs Caricom, reportedly said the bloc was ready to engage in talks. A small group of protesters outside called for reparatory justice.

stories.head: Reform UK councillor George Madgwick charged with 35 offences
stories.stand: The alleged offences date from 2008 to 2021 in Portsmouth and Wales; he is due at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 25 November.
stories.say: Hampshire councillor George Madgwick has been charged with 35 offences, including 12 counts of rape, involving four complainants. Reform UK has suspended him.
body: George Madgwick, 37, a Reform UK councillor in Hampshire and Portsmouth, has been charged with 35 offences, the Crown Prosecution Service announced on Tuesday.

The charges include 12 counts of rape, two of assault by penetration and two of sexual assault, as well as indecent image offences involving children, stalking and making threats to kill. They relate to four complainants who were 16 or 17 at the time.
The alleged offences took place between 2008 and 2021 in Portsmouth and Wales. Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary began investigating in July 2025.
He was bailed to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates' Court on 25 November. Reform UK suspended him with immediate effect. The CPS said he has the right to a fair trial.

stories.head: MI5 will not face contempt action over false evidence to courts
stories.stand: The Lady Chief Justice said any action should follow police and CPS decisions, and further proceedings would duplicate an existing investigation.
stories.say: Senior judges will not bring contempt proceedings against MI5 over false evidence it gave courts about an informant. Its head, Sir Ken McCallum, said the agency fell badly short.
body: Three senior judges, led by Lady Chief Justice Baroness Carr, ruled on Tuesday not to start contempt of court proceedings against MI5, its director-general Sir Ken McCallum, or individual officers.

MI5 had falsely told courts, including in a 2022 case brought against the BBC and at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, that it had kept a policy of neither confirming nor denying that a man known as X was an informant.
The judges said proceedings would mostly duplicate findings by Sir John Goldring, who found serious and systemic failings at MI5. They said any action should follow police and CPS charging decisions.
Sir Ken said the ruling underlined MI5's serious failures and that the agency he leads fell badly short.

stories.head: Henry Nowak's family urge politicians not to exploit his murder
stories.stand: Two officers face gross misconduct investigation over his arrest as he lay dying; protests in Southampton turned violent after bodycam footage was released.
stories.say: The family of murdered student Henry Nowak have told politicians not to use his death for political ends. Shabana Mahmood says she has full confidence in the police watchdog.
body: The family of Henry Nowak, 18, a Southampton student stabbed to death in December 2025, have criticised politicians for using his death in political arguments. His mother, Lucy Ross, said she was not interested in their political game.
Vickrum Digwa, 23, was jailed for life with a minimum of 21 years for the murder. Police bodycam footage showed officers arresting Henry as he lay dying.
Protests in Southampton after the footage was released turned violent, and 12 police officers were injured. The family said the riots were not acceptable.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct is investigating two officers for potential gross misconduct. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she had full confidence in the watchdog.

stories.head: House price recovery pushed back to 2028, Savills forecasts
stories.stand: The estate agency forecasts 15.8% growth over five years to 2031, with London weakest at 8.1% and the North West strongest.
stories.say: Savills expects average UK house prices to fall 1.5% in 2027 and not recover until the second half of 2028, blaming the Middle East conflict for keeping mortgage rates high.
body: Estate agency Savills forecasts that average UK house prices will fall a further 1.5% in 2027. It does not expect a recovery until the second half of 2028.
Emily Williams, its director of residential research, said the drawn-out conflict in the Middle East had pushed back meaningful mortgage rate relief.
Over the five years to 2031, Savills expects prices to rise 15.8%. London is forecast to be weakest at 8.1%, with the North West strongest at 23.3%.
The firm expects Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool and Bristol to outperform.

stories.head: British lawyer Dapo Akande elected to International Court of Justice
stories.stand: He was one of five judges elected by the UN General Assembly and Security Council for nine-year terms starting in February 2027.
stories.say: Oxford professor Dapo Akande has been elected to the International Court of Justice, giving Britain a judge on the UN's top court for the first time in about nine years.
body: Dapo Akande, professor of public international law at Oxford, has been elected to the International Court of Justice, the government said on Tuesday.
Britain has had no judge on the court for almost a decade. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the result a clear signal to partners.
Akande was one of five judges elected, alongside candidates from France, Jordan, Singapore and Kenya. Candidates needed majorities in both the General Assembly and the Security Council.
The nine-year terms begin on 6 February 2027.

stories.head: Driver who dragged cyclist for more than a mile jailed for life
stories.stand: The 56-year-old headteacher was hit at a junction in Warburton in April; the judge said Richardson put escape ahead of a human life.
stories.say: Simon Richardson has been jailed for life, with a minimum of 25 years, for murdering a cyclist he dragged for more than a mile under his car in Greater Manchester.
body: Simon Richardson, 35, has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 25 years for murdering a cyclist in Greater Manchester.
The victim, a 56-year-old headteacher, was hit at a junction in Warburton on 20 April. He became trapped under Richardson's Volvo and was dragged for more than a mile.
A jury at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court convicted Richardson of murder on 30 October. He had denied knowing the man was under his car.
Mrs Justice Brunner said he had decided escaping the scene was more important than a human life. Prosecutors said he had 28 previous convictions.

stories.stand: Nine medical procedures were cancelled and a medevac transfer was aborted; Jersey Police are investigating.
stories.say: A military aircraft from the UK has landed in Jersey, believed to carry counter-drone technology, after illegal drone activity diverted several flights over two nights.
body: Illegal drone activity diverted several flights at Jersey Airport on Friday and Saturday evenings.
Nine planned medical procedures were cancelled and a medevac ambulance transfer was aborted. Loganair called the activity a serious criminal act.

Jersey's government said additional measures were in place but gave no details. Jersey Police said investigations were continuing.

stories.head: PSNI chief says Troubles claims are harming the force
stories.stand: The force paid £7.7m in settlements and £14.6m in legal costs over five years, he said at an event marking 25 years of the PSNI.
stories.say: Northern Ireland's chief constable Jon Boutcher says Troubles-era civil claims have had a huge detrimental impact on the PSNI, and has called for financial help with legacy cases.
body: Jon Boutcher, Chief Constable of the Police Service of Northern Ireland, said on Monday that legacy civil claims from the Troubles had a huge detrimental impact on the force.
He said the PSNI paid £7.7m in legacy compensation settlements and spent £14.6m on legal costs between July 2021 and July 2026.
He called for financial help with legacy cases. He said the PSNI budget was about £1bn, the same as in 2010.
He spoke at Queen's University Belfast during events marking 25 years of the PSNI, which replaced the Royal Ulster Constabulary in 2001.

stories.head: Democrats projected to win control of both houses of Congress
stories.stand: US networks project a Democratic sweep of Congress, though seat totals were still being counted early on Wednesday.
stories.say: Democrats are projected to take both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterms, flipping Senate seats in Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa.
body: CBS News projected late on Tuesday that Democrats had won a majority in the Senate. CBS, ABC News, NBC News and CNN also projected that Democrats would take control of the House.

Republicans went into the election holding the Senate 53-47, so Democrats needed a net gain of four seats. CBS lists Democratic gains in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina, South Carolina and Ohio, while the party held Georgia and New Hampshire.

NBC News projected that Democrats would win 244 House seats, above the 218 needed for a majority, according to El Tiempo. Reported Democratic gains include districts in North Carolina, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Kentucky.
Counting continues in many races, and CBS says the size of the new Senate majority remains to be seen. Final totals may take days.

stories.head: Democrats win Texas Senate seat and governorship
stories.stand: Democrats won both of Texas's top races, ending decades of Republican dominance in the state.
stories.say: Texas has elected James Talarico to the Senate, beating Ken Paxton, while Gina Hinojosa ousted Governor Greg Abbott. Texas had not elected a Democratic senator since 1988.
body: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, according to projections by CBS News, NBC News and CNN. Texas had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988.

Talarico, 37, is a former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian who campaigned on corruption and costs. Paxton, the 63-year-old state attorney general, had beaten Senator John Cornyn in the Republican runoff after a late endorsement from President Trump.
Paxton was impeached by the Texas House in 2023 and acquitted by the state Senate. CBS says spending in the race passed half a billion dollars, the most for any Texas Senate contest.

In the governor's race, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, a state representative from Austin, defeated Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term. Fox News says she will be the first Latina governor of Texas. CBS says she is the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards.

stories.head: Democrats flip Senate seats in the Carolinas, Ohio and Kansas
stories.stand: Several Senate seats in states Donald Trump won in 2024 changed hands, including some held by Republicans for decades.
stories.say: Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and Adam Hamilton in Kansas all took Republican-held Senate seats in Tuesday's vote.
body: Former North Carolina governor Roy Cooper defeated Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, for the seat of retiring Senator Thom Tillis. Al Jazeera says he is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from the state since 2008.

In South Carolina, paediatrician Annie Andrews beat Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late Lindsey Graham, who died in July. CBS News says the state had not elected a Democratic senator since 1998.
In Ohio, former senator Sherrod Brown, 73, defeated Jon Husted, who was appointed to replace JD Vance. CBS says no senator since 1988 had won back a seat after losing re-election.
In Kansas, Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton ousted Senator Roger Marshall. CBS notes the last Democrat elected to the Senate from Kansas won in 1932.

stories.head: Democrats win governor races in Ohio, Iowa and California
stories.stand: Democrats picked up governorships in two states Donald Trump won comfortably in 2024 and held California.
stories.say: Amy Acton beat Vivek Ramaswamy for Ohio governor, Rob Sand won in Iowa, and Xavier Becerra will succeed Gavin Newsom in California, according to CBS News projections.
body: CBS News projected that Democrat Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio. Acton, 60, led the state health department during Covid-19. Trump won Ohio by 11 points in 2024.
Ramaswamy's campaign ran a $4 million advert in October featuring Acton's estranged mother. CBS says Democrats and many Republicans condemned it, while Trump said he supported it.
In Iowa, state auditor Rob Sand beat Republican Zach Lahn. CBS says he will be the first Democrat elected governor there since 2006.

In California, former health secretary Xavier Becerra defeated Republican Steve Hilton, who had Trump's endorsement. CBS says Becerra will be the state's first Latino governor since Romualdo Pacheco, more than 150 years ago.

stories.head: Midterms bring firsts in Georgia, Florida and the Senate
stories.stand: Winners in Georgia, Florida and New Hampshire set historical firsts, from both parties.
stories.say: Keisha Lance Bottoms becomes the first Black woman elected a US governor, Byron Donalds Florida's first Black governor, and Chris Pappas the first openly gay man in the Senate.
body: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, won Georgia's governorship. Al Jazeera says she is the first Black woman to win a US governor's race. She beat Republican billionaire Rick Jackson, who spent over $200 million of his own money.

In Florida, the Fox News Decision Desk projected that Republican Byron Donalds beat Democrat David Jolly. Fox says he will be Florida's first Black governor and the first Black Republican elected governor in US history.

In New Hampshire, Democrat Chris Pappas beat former Republican senator John E. Sununu to succeed Jeanne Shaheen. He will be the first openly gay man in the Senate. Tammy Baldwin became the first openly gay person elected to the Senate in 2012.

stories.head: Trump says he will accept results but blames Republican candidates
stories.stand: The president signalled he would use his veto against a Democratic Congress while deflecting blame for the losses.
stories.say: President Trump says he will accept the midterm results and work with Democrats, but blamed his party's candidates and said his veto gives him the ultimate power.
body: Donald Trump told The New York Times he was willing to accept the midterm results and would work with Democrats, AFP reports. He also shifted blame to Republican candidates.

On Truth Social he wrote that he was not on the ballot and would otherwise have won. A White House official told AFP that candidate quality matters. Trump said Greg Abbott would not have lost in Texas had he not become a RINO.

Speaking to CBS News by phone on Tuesday, Trump said he had the ultimate power of the veto, Fox News reports. He said vetoes usually push opponents to make a deal after a couple of months. He later posted an image of a MAGA hat reading VETO.
Fox says Trump made more than 27 rallies in October. He will face a Democratic-controlled Congress for his last two years in office.

stories.head: Midterm voters unhappy with Trump and focused on the economy, poll finds
stories.stand: The AP Voter Poll suggests the economy, democracy and corruption drove the vote, with young and Hispanic voters moving away from Republicans.
stories.say: A survey of about 80,000 voters found roughly 6 in 10 disapprove of President Trump, with the economy the top issue and young voters swinging strongly to Democrats.
body: The AP Voter Poll surveyed about 80,000 voters in all 50 states. It was conducted by SSRS for The Associated Press and several networks, including CBS News and Fox News Media.
About 6 in 10 voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency. About 4 in 10 said they voted to express opposition to him, against just under 2 in 10 who voted to support him.
About 4 in 10 named the economy as the top issue and about 3 in 10 named democracy. Roughly half called corruption and the cost of living crucial to their House vote.
About 7 in 10 voters under 30 backed the Democratic House candidate. About a third of Hispanic voters backed Republicans, down from about 4 in 10 who voted for Trump in 2024.

stories.head: UK and EU agree draft deal to cut red tape on food exports
stories.stand: A draft agreement on food and farming trade would remove many border checks in return for the UK following EU standards.
stories.say: Britain and the EU have agreed a draft deal to scrap many post-Brexit checks on food exports, with the UK following EU food rules. The government puts the gain at £5.1bn a year.
body: The UK and the EU have agreed a draft text of about 200 pages on sanitary and phytosanitary rules covering food and farm trade. It was circulated to EU member states ahead of a UK-EU summit later in November.

The deal would remove many certificates, fees and border inspections introduced after Brexit. Ministers say it would restore exports of products such as sausages, burgers and shellfish, and bring back pet passports.
In return, Britain would follow EU animal, plant and food rules as they evolve, known as dynamic alignment. The government estimates the deal could eventually bring £5.1bn a year to the economy.

Drafts on linking emissions trading and a youth travel scheme were circulated alongside it. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of creating confusion about his aims on Europe.

stories.head: MPs warn Parliament risks a catastrophic event without urgent repairs
stories.stand: The Public Accounts Committee says delays to restoring the Palace of Westminster are driving up costs and risks.
stories.say: A committee of MPs says each year of delay to repairing the Palace of Westminster adds £420m to the bill, and warns of the risk of a catastrophic event such as a fire.
body: The Public Accounts Committee published a report on Wednesday on the Palace of Westminster. It warns of a risk of a catastrophic event that could cause injury or disrupt democracy.
It says each year of delay adds £420m to the programme's lifetime costs. Weekly maintenance is expected to rise from £1.5m to £2m.

Two options are under consideration. Moving everyone out would cost up to £15.6bn and take up to 24 years. A partial move would cost up to £39bn and take up to 61 years. A first phase is capped at £3bn, with works due to start in 2032.

Committee chair Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown cited the risk of a fire like that at Notre Dame. A Parliament spokesperson said that without action the building faces managed decline at best. MPs first voted to leave the building for repairs in 2018.

stories.head: South Africans vote in local elections amid anger over services
stories.stand: The municipal vote is seen as a test for the ANC ahead of national elections in 2029.
stories.say: South Africans vote for local councils on Wednesday, with the ANC expected to lose more support amid water outages in Johannesburg and violence in KwaZulu-Natal.
body: South Africa holds local government elections on Wednesday 4 November, a public holiday. Voting stations are open from 7am to 9pm.

The ANC, the largest party in the national unity government, is expected to lose more support, Africanews reports. Johannesburg has faced severe water outages since 19 October, and about 800 people fell ill in Tshwane after drinking tap water.

Police have recorded 21 election-related cases since 1 November, including murder, intimidation and arson, with arrests in six, Daily Maverick reports. More than 300 voting stations are classed as high-risk, nearly half of them in KwaZulu-Natal.
Where no party wins a majority, parties will have to form coalitions to choose mayors.

stories.head: Poland's clash over its constitutional court deepens
stories.stand: A judge's suspension of the tribunal's leaders has pitted the president against the government and prompted ambassadors to resign.
stories.say: Poland's row over its constitutional court has escalated after a judge suspended the court's leaders, with President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk on opposite sides.
body: On Friday 30 October, a judge elected by parliament in March suspended the president and vice-president of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal for one month. Fox News reported the move.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government backed the move as a way to restore judicial independence. President Karol Nawrocki, backed by the Law and Justice party, turned back from a trip to Senegal. His office called the government's actions legally unfounded.
Tusk said the president should recognise the judges parliament had elected. At least three Polish ambassadors resigned in protest, including the envoy to the UN.
Police detained three people after protesters clashed with officers outside the court. Parliamentary elections are due in about a year.

stories.head: US stock futures and dollar fall as Democrats gain in midterms
stories.stand: Investors sold US shares and bought Treasury bonds as early counts pointed to strong Democratic gains in Congress.
stories.say: US stock futures slid and the dollar weakened on Wednesday as early midterm results pointed to Democratic gains, while Japan's Nikkei fell 3% and Treasury yields dropped.
body: US stock futures fell in Asian trading on Wednesday as early midterm results pointed to Democratic gains in Congress. Futures on the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell further than those on the S&P 500.
Investors moved into US government bonds. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 6 basis points to 4.906%. The dollar weakened, and sterling rose 0.37% to $1.3464.
In Asia, Japan's Nikkei fell 3% as it reopened after a holiday, and South Korea's Kospi lost 1.6%. More than $1.48bn had been wagered on the elections in prediction markets.
Charu Chanana of Saxo said markets seemed to be pricing in a stronger Democratic showing than expected. She added that lower bond yields could limit the sell-off.

stories.head: Oil holds near four-week low as traders weigh US-Iran talks
stories.stand: Brent crude traded around $103 a barrel on Wednesday after sliding to its lowest level in nearly four weeks on Tuesday.
stories.say: Brent crude traded around 103 dollars a barrel on Wednesday after sliding to a near four-week low, as traders weighed Qatar-led talks between the US and Iran.
body: Oil prices edged lower in Asian trading on Wednesday. Brent crude was around $103 a barrel and US crude, WTI, was around $95.60.
Brent fell more than 1% on Tuesday to its lowest level in nearly four weeks. That followed a slump of 7.63% on Monday, when it settled at $104.77.

Traders have been weighing Qatar's mediation between Washington and Tehran. A senior Iranian official said the two sides remained far from a deal. Trump told the Financial Times the US had no immediate plans for further strikes on Iran.
Industry data from the API showed US crude stocks fell more than expected in the week to 30 October. That limited the fall in prices.

stories.head: UK plans default retirement income for private-sector pension savers
stories.stand: Ministers want schemes to turn savings pots into a regular income by default, while providers warn savers must keep the freedom to choose.
stories.say: Pension schemes would have to offer savers a regular income in retirement by default under plans set out on Tuesday by pensions minister Torsten Bell, covering about 17 million workers.
body: Pensions minister Torsten Bell set out plans on Tuesday to make pension schemes offer savers a regular retirement income by default. The government calls the plan Guided Retirement.

About 17 million private-sector workers saving into a pension would be given the option. The Department for Work and Pensions says about 46% of first-time pot withdrawals in 2025/26 emptied the whole pot.

One route is a new collective scheme that pools risk between savers. City AM notes these schemes do not legally guarantee an income, which can fall if funds underperform. Savers could still choose another option.
A consultation runs from 3 November to 22 December 2026. Providers including Quilter and Standard Life said a default should not stop people choosing a different approach.

stories.head: Virgin Media O2 to cut jobs and halt further full-fibre upgrades
stories.stand: The UK broadband and mobile group plans £800m of annual savings by 2029, including about £300m from cutting its workforce.
stories.say: Virgin Media O2 is cutting jobs as part of a plan to save 800 million pounds a year by 2029, and will stop full-fibre upgrades beyond those already promised.
body: Virgin Media O2 plans to save about £800m a year by 2029, with roughly £400m expected in 2027. About £300m will come from cutting staff, around 30% of its people costs.
The company did not give a number for job losses. It will stop full-fibre upgrades beyond existing commitments. Instead, a cheaper upgrade will bring 2Gbps speeds to most of its network in 2027.
Third-quarter revenue fell 5.7% to £2.4bn, and adjusted EBITDA fell 2.6% to £995m. The group, owned by Liberty Global and Telefonica, has more than £22bn of debt, City AM reported.
Chief executive Lutz Schuler said standing still was not an option. The Communication Workers Union warned that losing experienced staff could hurt customer service.

stories.head: UK meat suppliers among firms hit by European fridge cyber attacks
stories.stand: The National Cyber Security Centre says vulnerable refrigeration technology was exploited in a small number of incidents in Britain.
stories.say: Britain's cyber security agency says hackers exploited refrigeration systems in a small number of UK cases, with some independent meat suppliers affected but no stock lost.
body: The National Cyber Security Centre said on Tuesday that vulnerable refrigeration technology had been exploited in a small number of incidents in Britain.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers, which represents more than 300 businesses, said some members were affected but none lost stock. NCSC chief Richard Horne said small meat-processing firms were targeted and the impact was minimal.

Across Europe, hackers have switched supermarket fridges into defrost mode, forcing retailers to throw away food. Attacks have hit at least 11 countries. Horne said it was too early to say who was responsible.
Researchers at Bridewell found more than 800 fridge interfaces linked to British retailers reachable over the internet. The British Retail Consortium said retailers were working with the NCSC.

Chief executive Josh D'Amaro plans to spend part of the savings on film and TV, technology, theme parks and cruise ships, the reports say. He succeeded Bob Iger in March 2026.
Disney had about 231,000 employees at the end of fiscal 2025. It cut about 1,000 roles in April and made further cuts in technology and human resources in September.
Disney did not immediately respond to a request for comment from TheWrap.

stories.head: Uber loses High Court fight over $81m payroll tax bill in Australia
stories.stand: Australia's top court ruled on Wednesday that payments to Uber drivers in New South Wales count as wages for payroll tax purposes.
stories.say: Australia's High Court has ruled that Uber owes 81 million dollars in New South Wales payroll tax, finding that fares paid to its drivers count as wages.
body: Australia's High Court on Wednesday dismissed Uber's appeal against an $81m payroll tax bill in New South Wales. Six of the seven judges ruled against the company, according to AAP.

The court found that fares paid to drivers count as wages under payroll tax law. The bill covers payments from the 2015 to 2020 financial years. Uber must also pay the revenue commissioner's legal costs.
Uber had argued it was only a payment collection agent. It said it respected the decision but urged states to update payroll tax laws for digital platforms.
The Transport Workers Union called the ruling a win for workers. NSW Finance Minister Courtney Houssos said Uber should pay its fair share.

stories.head: Half of UK small firms expect to be worse off after Budget, survey finds
stories.stand: A Capital on Tap survey found 52% of small and medium firms expect to lose out, and 42% said they would raise prices.
stories.say: Just over half of the small firms surveyed by Capital on Tap expect to be worse off after John Healey's Budget, with minimum wage rises the most commonly cited cost.
body: A survey of small and medium-sized firms by lender Capital on Tap found 52% expect to be worse off after Chancellor John Healey's Budget. Only 10% expect to be better off.
One in three named minimum wage rises as the biggest hit to their finances. In response, 42% said they would raise prices and 27% would put investment on hold.
The Centre for Policy Studies estimated the yearly cost of a full-time minimum wage worker rose by at least £4,462 from 2024 to 2027.
Official forecasts published with the Budget cut expected UK growth for 2026 to 1% from 1.6%, City AM reported.

stories.head: UK regulators float lighter rules to help credit unions grow
stories.stand: The Prudential Regulation Authority and the FCA set out nine options, including simpler rules for small credit unions and a path to building society status.
stories.say: UK regulators are asking for views on lighter rules for small credit unions and a new route for them to become building societies, in a paper published on Tuesday.
body: The Prudential Regulation Authority and the Financial Conduct Authority published a discussion paper on Tuesday on how credit unions are regulated.
It sets out nine options. They include fewer audit and paperwork demands for smaller credit unions and more flexible capital rules for larger ones.
The regulators also suggest a route for credit unions to convert into building societies, and a review of whether FCA fees could be cut.
Credit unions are member-owned lenders that focus on savings and personal loans. They have more than two million members in the UK.

stories.head: South African petrol falls 1 cent a litre as diesel drops over R1
stories.stand: Temporary fuel levy cuts eased pump prices from Wednesday, but higher oil prices and a weaker rand limited the cut for petrol.
stories.say: South Africa's petrol price fell by just 1 cent a litre on Wednesday, while diesel dropped by more than one rand, as temporary fuel levy cuts offset higher oil prices.
body: South Africa's petrol price fell by 1 cent a litre from Wednesday, the mineral resources department announced. Wholesale diesel fell by between R1.10 and R1.20 a litre.
Temporary fuel levy cuts of R3 a litre for diesel and R1.50 for petrol apply until 1 December. Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana has put the cost of the relief at about R10bn.
The department said the average Brent crude price rose from $101 to $108 a barrel in the review period. The rand also weakened against the dollar.
The slate levy, which covers past under-recoveries on fuel, rose by more than 48 cents to 135.84 cents a litre, Daily Maverick reported.

stories.head: NASA's Swift telescope set to fall back to Earth after 22 years
stories.stand: The gamma-ray burst hunter, built for a two-year mission, lost altitude faster than expected and was shut down on 20 October.
stories.say: NASA's Swift observatory was predicted to re-enter the atmosphere early on Wednesday, after a 30 million dollar rescue attempt failed. NASA says most of it should burn up.
body: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory was expected to re-enter Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday 4 November. The US Space Force predicted re-entry at about 3:30am Eastern time, with a margin of several hours.

NASA says most of the spacecraft should burn up, though some parts are likely to survive. It puts the risk of harm to anyone on Earth at about 1 in 2,100. Any debris is most likely to fall into the ocean.
Swift launched in 2004 on a planned two-year mission and operated for about 22 years. It detected more than 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and studied more than 1,400 exploding stars.

NASA paid Katalyst Space $30 million to boost Swift's orbit with a robotic craft called LINK, but the attempt failed and was called off in August. Strong solar activity pulled Swift down faster than expected, and it was shut down on 20 October.

stories.head: NASA asks companies for ideas to keep Hubble in orbit
stories.stand: A request for information issued on 29 October covers raising Hubble's orbit, servicing it, or guiding it to a controlled re-entry.
stories.say: NASA has asked companies how they might boost or service the Hubble Space Telescope, which is on course to fall from orbit in 2033 or 2034. Responses are due on 30 November.
body: NASA issued a request for information on 29 October asking industry for ideas on servicing the Hubble Space Telescope. Options include raising its orbit, upgrading it, or a safe controlled re-entry.
Atmospheric drag is slowly lowering Hubble, which has no engine of its own. NASA projects an uncontrolled re-entry in 2033 or 2034, and says any intervention would be needed by 2032.
Responses are due by 30 November. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement on 30 October that the agency should look at every reasonable chance to keep Hubble working.
Hubble launched in 1990 and was serviced five times by space shuttle crews, most recently in 2009. The request comes as NASA's smaller Swift telescope falls back to Earth after a failed rescue.

stories.head: Voyager 1 two weeks from becoming one light-day from Earth
stories.stand: Launched in 1977, the probe will be about 25.9 billion km away, so a signal takes 24 hours to reach it.
stories.say: Voyager 1 is due on 18 November to become the first human-made object a full light-day from Earth. NASA says it recently regained contact after a two-day silence.
body: NASA's Voyager 1 is expected to reach one light-day from Earth on 18 November. It will be about 25.9 billion km away, further than any other human-made object.
At that distance, a radio signal takes 24 hours to travel each way. The spacecraft launched in 1977 and has been flying for more than 49 years.

NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory said contact was lost on 18 and 19 October and returned on 20 October. One set of thrusters stopped working and the craft switched to backups; the cause is not yet known.
Its power supply falls by about 4 watts a year, and engineers have switched off equipment to save energy. Mission manager Kareem Badaruddin said the team was relieved to be back in contact.

stories.head: Europe's Hera probe sees DART's target asteroid for the first time
stories.stand: Hera is closing in on the double asteroid that NASA's DART craft struck in 2022 to test deflecting a space rock.
stories.say: Europe's Hera spacecraft has picked out the small asteroid Dimorphos beside its larger partner Didymos, in an image from 1,280 km away. Detailed pictures are due on 25 November.
body: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has photographed the asteroid Dimorphos as a separate object from its larger partner, Didymos, for the first time. The image was taken on 18 October from 1,280 km away.
Dimorphos, about 151 metres across, fills roughly one pixel. ESA's Michael Kueppers said the smaller asteroid was now visible for the first time.

NASA's DART spacecraft hit Dimorphos on 26 September 2022, shortening its orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes. Hera will examine the impact site, release two small CubeSats and may attempt a landing.
ESA says the first detailed images of Dimorphos will be released on 25 November. The asteroid pair is about 197 million km from Earth.

stories.head: Three NASA astronauts vote in US midterms from the space station
stories.stand: Encrypted electronic ballots travel by NASA satellite and Mission Control to the county clerk in Texas.
stories.say: Three NASA astronauts on the International Space Station, Anil Menon, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins, cast ballots in the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
body: NASA astronauts Anil Menon, Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins voted in the US midterm elections from the International Space Station on 3 November, Space.com reported.

Each filled in an electronic ballot. It is encrypted and sent via NASA's satellite network and Mission Control in Houston to the county clerk. Most NASA astronauts are registered in Harris County, Texas.
Texas passed a law allowing voting from space in 1997. NASA astronaut David Wolf was the first to use it, voting from Russia's Mir station that year.
Seven people are currently on the station. Delaney and Watkins arrived on SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which launched on 1 October.

stories.head: NASA crew leaves simulated Mars habitat after 378 days
stories.stand: The second CHAPEA crew lived in a 3D-printed habitat at Johnson Space Center, coping with delays and limited supplies.
stories.say: Four volunteers have left NASA's simulated Mars base in Houston after 378 days sealed inside. The agency says the data will help plan a future Moon base and Mars missions.
body: The four-person crew of NASA's second CHAPEA mission left their simulated Mars habitat on 31 October. They had lived inside since 19 October 2025, a mission of 378 days.
The crew were Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, Matthew Montgomery and James Spicer. Their 1,700 square foot habitat is 3D-printed and sits at Johnson Space Center in Houston.
During the mission they grew crops, managed limited supplies, dealt with communication delays and carried out simulated spacewalks.
NASA says the results will inform designs for a future Moon base and plans for Mars missions. The crew face two weeks of post-mission tests.

stories.head: Webb finds dusty ice in interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS
stories.stand: A study in The Astrophysical Journal Letters says the comet's ice resembles some icy bodies beyond Neptune.
stories.say: Webb telescope data suggest the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS holds water ice mixed with dark dust in tiny grains, unlike comets from our own solar system.
body: Water ice in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS is mixed with dark, rocky material in very small grains, according to a study using the James Webb Space Telescope.

The research, led by Silvia Protopapa of the Southwest Research Institute, appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on 26 October. Webb observed the comet three times between August 2025 and April 2026.
Some water-ice signals were weak or missing. The researchers say this differs from solar system comets but resembles some icy objects beyond Neptune.
3I/ATLAS is the third known object to enter the solar system from another star system. The authors suggest planet-building ice grains vary in dust content around different stars.

stories.head: Rocket Lab launches Japanese radar satellite on 99th mission
stories.stand: The launch for Japanese company iQPS placed an Earth-observing radar satellite about 575 km above Earth.
stories.say: Rocket Lab's Electron rocket has put a Japanese radar satellite into orbit from New Zealand, on the company's 99th mission and the 90th flight of Electron.
body: Rocket Lab launched an Electron rocket from its New Zealand site on 2 November, US time. It carried a synthetic aperture radar satellite for the Japanese company iQPS.
The satellite was deployed into low Earth orbit at about 575 km, roughly 56 minutes after lift-off, Space.com reported.
It was Rocket Lab's 99th mission overall and the 90th Electron launch. It was also the company's 10th launch for iQPS, which is building a constellation of radar satellites.

stories.head: Museum frogs point to fungus behind Brazil's 1980s amphibian crash
stories.stand: None of the specimens collected before 1979 carried the fungus; more than half of those from the 1980s did.
stories.say: Preserved frogs from Brazil's Atlantic Forest show the chytrid fungus arrived around the time local amphibians crashed in the early 1980s, a Smithsonian-led study says.
body: A Smithsonian-led team tested more than 370 preserved amphibians from 17 species collected at the Boraceia Biological Station in Brazil's Atlantic Forest. Frog numbers there fell sharply between 1979 and 1982.
None of the specimens collected before 1979 carried the chytrid fungus. More than half of those collected in the 1980s tested positive, pointing to the disease as the likely cause.
Oddly, the species that declined most were rarely found infected. The researchers suggest the most vulnerable frogs died before they could be collected.
Surveys between 2022 and 2024 found 12 of the 17 species again. The study, led by Jack Boyette, appears in Molecular Ecology and involved Penn State and the University of Sao Paulo.

stories.head: Genomes trace Native Hawaiians' closest kin to Rapa Nui
stories.stand: The study in Science says Polynesia was settled by small groups, leaving genetic bottlenecks that can raise the risk of rare diseases.
stories.say: A Stanford-led genetic study says Native Hawaiians are most closely related to the people of Rapa Nui, with Mangareva in French Polynesia a possible shared launch point.
body: Native Hawaiians are most closely related to the people of Rapa Nui, also known as Easter Island, according to a genetic study published in Science. The islands lie thousands of kilometres apart.
The researchers, including Alexander Ioannidis of Stanford University, suggest Mangareva in French Polynesia may have been the launch point for both populations.
The team analysed genomes from more than 1,000 people in French Polynesia, 12 from Rapa Nui and data on Native Hawaiians, Samoans and Tongans.
The study says islands were settled by small groups, causing repeated genetic bottlenecks. It identifies variants linked to inherited conditions affecting the eyes and kidneys.

stories.head: Extinct giant ground bird named from Flores 'hobbit' cave
stories.stand: Megapodius rokusi, known from one leg bone, lived on the Indonesian island roughly 190,000 to 120,000 years ago.
stories.say: Scientists have named a new extinct bird from the Flores cave where the so-called hobbit humans were found. The megapode weighed about 3.9 kg, several times more than its living relative.
body: Researchers have described a new extinct megapode, a chicken-like ground bird, from Liang Bua cave on the Indonesian island of Flores. The cave is where Homo floresiensis was found.
Named Megapodius rokusi, it is known from a single lower leg bone excavated in 2009. Sediments around it date to roughly 190,000 to 120,000 years ago.
The bird is estimated to have weighed about 3.9 kg, several times more than the living orange-footed megapode. It is the first fossil megapode described from Wallacea.
It is named after Indonesian zooarchaeologist Rokus Due Awe. The study, led by Hanneke Meijer of the University Museum of Bergen, appeared in Alcheringa.

stories.head: Star pile-ups could seed early black holes, UCLA study suggests
stories.stand: Simulations published in The Astrophysical Journal offer one route to the unexpectedly early supermassive black holes seen by Webb.
stories.say: UCLA astrophysicists say repeated star collisions in crowded early clusters could build giant stars that collapse into black hole seeds, and may explain Webb's Little Red Dots.
body: Dense star clusters in the early universe could have produced the seeds of supermassive black holes, according to simulations by UCLA researchers Claire Williams and Smadar Naoz.
Their study in The Astrophysical Journal finds slow collisions between stars can lead to repeated mergers. These build very massive stars that may collapse into black holes.
Collisions that destroy stars could also pile up dense gas around a black hole. The authors suggest this might explain Little Red Dots, compact objects seen by the James Webb Space Telescope.
Webb has found supermassive black holes earlier in cosmic history than theory predicted. The Little Red Dots explanation is presented as a hypothesis.

stories.head: Sahara meteorite is oldest Martian igneous rock yet found
stories.stand: Teghaza 001 also shows signs of having been altered by water on Mars, the researchers say.
stories.say: A meteorite found in Mali's Sahara is a piece of Mars at least 4.1 billion years old, researchers report in Science, making it the oldest Martian igneous rock found so far.
body: A meteorite found in the Sahara in Mali is a piece of Mars at least 4.1 billion years old, according to a study published in Science on 29 October.
Called Teghaza 001, it weighs 798.5 g across eight fragments. Dating of zircon crystals gave an age of about 4.11 billion years.
Carl Agee of the University of New Mexico called it the oldest Martian igneous rock ever found by a huge margin. The study was led by Yang Liu of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
Its minerals and oxygen isotopes suggest it interacted with water on Mars. The researchers think it came from the southern highlands, near the Hellas impact basin.

stories.head: NHS tests multi-cancer blood checks in 200 GP surgeries
stories.stand: The government-backed trial will check whether blood tests help GPs spot abdominal cancers earlier before any decision on a national rollout.
stories.say: A trial called STRIDE-RCT will offer 20,000 patients over 45 with symptoms such as bloating a blood test looking for 13 cancers, at 200 GP surgeries in England.
body: A government-backed trial will test whether blood tests can help GPs in England spot abdominal cancers earlier. The STRIDE-RCT trial involves 20,000 patients at 200 GP surgeries.

Patients over 45 with symptoms such as bloating, stomach cramps, heartburn, diarrhoea or constipation will be offered the test. It looks for tumour DNA and proteins in the blood, uses artificial intelligence and suggests where a cancer may start. It covers 13 cancers, including bowel, pancreatic, ovarian and prostate.

Tests from three companies will be assessed, most of them developed at the University of Birmingham. GPs will also record how strongly they suspect cancer, so the tests can be judged against clinical judgement.

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper called the trial world-first. Professor Peter Johnson, NHS England's director for cancer, said these cancers are hard to catch early because symptoms resemble less serious conditions. Any national rollout depends on the results.

stories.head: US-bound passengers must now declare they have not been in Congo
stories.stand: The rule, aimed at the Ebola outbreak, applies to all nationalities including US citizens and runs until 18 December unless changed.
stories.say: Every passenger flying into the United States must now sign a form saying they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the past 21 days, under a rule that began on Tuesday.
body: A new US rule took effect on Tuesday night for all international passengers flying to the United States. They must declare they have not been in the Democratic Republic of Congo in the previous 21 days.
It applies to all nationalities, including US citizens returning home. Changing planes at an airport in Congo also counts. Travellers who were in Congo within 21 days cannot board.
Medical Daily reports that airlines must refuse boarding to anyone without a completed form. The order runs until 18 December unless officials change it.
The measure is a response to the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak centred on Congo. The CDC says the risk to Americans is low.

stories.head: Watchdog bans four ads for weight loss pills
stories.stand: The UK regulator said ads can break the rules even when no medicine is named, if the overall impression points to a prescription drug.
stories.say: The Advertising Standards Authority has banned four ads from Voy, Juniper and MedExpress, saying they promoted prescription-only weight loss pills to the public without naming them.
body: The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) has banned four ads for prescription-only weight loss pills. Two were from Voy, one from Juniper and one from MedExpress.
The ASA said Voy's bus and video-on-demand ads were likely to be read as promoting oral Wegovy tablets. Small print referring to a food supplement did not change that impression, it said.
The Juniper and MedExpress ads were banned even though neither named a medicine. ASA investigations manager Catherine Drewett said advertisers must consider the overall impression their ads create.

Voy said it had withdrawn its ads during the investigation and would not run them again. MedExpress said its ad was removed after an internal review. The ASA said it monitors the sector using AI tools.

stories.head: Births at Newry's Daisy Hill hospital to move to Craigavon
stories.stand: The Northern Ireland trust says the move to Craigavon Area Hospital is temporary and is driven by the safety of women and babies.
stories.say: Babies will no longer be delivered at Daisy Hill Hospital in Newry from the twenty-third of November, after the Southern Trust said it could not recruit enough consultant obstetricians.
body: Births and inpatient maternity care at Daisy Hill Hospital in Newry will move to Craigavon Area Hospital from Monday 23 November. The Southern Trust board approved the plan at a public meeting on Tuesday.

The trust said it could not secure enough consultant obstetricians to run the service safely. Several consultants have retired or resigned, and recruitment has not filled the posts. Down News reports that up to five more permanent consultants are needed.
The trust describes the change as temporary. Chief executive Steve Spoerry said the priority was the safety of women and babies and that the trust hopes to restore the service.
Antenatal and postnatal care will continue at Daisy Hill, according to the Irish News. Campaigners have opposed the move, mainly over longer journeys.

stories.head: Adults diagnosed with autism now more likely to have anxiety, study finds
stories.stand: A study of UK and Swedish records in BMJ Mental Health found the profile of adults diagnosed as autistic has changed sharply since 2010.
stories.say: New adult autism diagnoses in the UK rose from 6 to 64 per 100,000 people between 2010 and 2023, a study finds, and more of those diagnosed already had anxiety, ADHD or depression.
body: A study in BMJ Mental Health found new autism diagnoses in UK adults rose from 6 to 64 per 100,000 between 2010 and 2023. It used UK GP records and Swedish national registers.

Among newly diagnosed UK adults, the share with a previous anxiety diagnosis rose from about 29% to 58%. Prior epilepsy fell from 10% to 4%. Earlier diagnoses of ADHD and depression became more common.
The steepest rise in the UK was among 16- to 20-year-olds, women and white people. In Sweden, adult diagnoses rose from 43 to 65 per 100,000 between 2010 and 2021.

The researchers, from the University of Bristol and an NHS mental health trust, said the study cannot explain the changes. Dr Monique Botha of Durham University said they may reflect past gaps in diagnosis.

stories.head: Spain ends 24-hour shifts for junior doctors in training
stories.stand: The royal decree approved on Tuesday also limits residents' working week and protects their pay during sick and parental leave.
stories.say: Spain's government has approved a decree ending 24-hour on-call shifts for resident doctors, capping them at 17 hours in a row with no more than four a month.
body: Spain's Council of Ministers approved a royal decree on Tuesday that ends 24-hour on-call shifts for resident doctors in training. Their continuous working time is now capped at 17 hours.
Residents can do up to four such shifts a month. Ordinary and on-call hours combined may not exceed 45 a week, averaged over a quarter. Residents must get at least 12 hours' rest between shifts.
Secretary of State for Health Javier Padilla said there would be no exceptions for weekends, according to elDiario.es. The decree also protects residents' pay during sick leave and parental leave.
elDiario.es reports that pay changes apply from 1 January 2027 and the new working hours from 1 September 2027. The decree replaces rules dating from 2003.

stories.head: France pulls 15 ranges of faulty condoms sold across the EU
stories.stand: French consumer authorities say users of affected condoms should get tested for sexually transmitted infections and take a pregnancy test if a period is late.
stories.say: France has suspended sales of 15 ranges of ultra-thin condoms from a Malaysian maker after tests found defects that could make them burst; Euronews puts the recall at about 7 million.
body: France has suspended the sale and import of 15 condom ranges made by a Malaysian manufacturer, Richter Rubber Technology. The products were sold across the EU under several brand names.

France's consumer protection authority, the DGCCRF, said laboratory tests found manufacturing defects in the latex that could cause the condoms to burst or tear. Euronews reports that about 7 million condoms are affected.
The order was published in France's Official Journal on 30 October. The suspension lasts one year and can be renewed.
Anyone who used an affected condom is advised to get screened for sexually transmitted infections. A pregnancy test is advised if a period is late.

stories.head: A quarter of teenagers get no days of proper exercise, WHO says
stories.stand: The WHO report, based on surveys of more than 3.2 million adolescents in 140 countries, says no country is on track to meet its 2030 target.
stories.say: A World Health Organization report says 25% of 11 to 17-year-olds had no day with an hour of moderate or vigorous activity in the past week, with little change since 2010.
body: The World Health Organization published a report on Wednesday on physical activity among adolescents aged 11 to 17. It draws on 389 surveys covering more than 3.2 million young people in 140 countries and territories.
It found that 25% reported no day in the previous week with at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity. Only 14% were active on all seven days.
The WHO says levels have changed little since 2010 and girls are consistently less active than boys. No country is on track to cut physical inactivity by 15% by 2030.
The report calls for safe, affordable opportunities for young people to be active and for action to close the gender gap.

stories.head: South Africa's mpox cases reach 26 this year
stories.stand: Most cases are the sub-clade Ib strain, seven people have been hospitalised and no deaths have been reported this year.
stories.say: South Africa has confirmed 26 mpox cases this year, 20 of them since August, most in the Western Cape; the health department says nearly 3,900 vaccine doses remain in stock.
body: South Africa had confirmed 26 mpox cases in 2026 by 27 October, with 20 detected since August. The figures come from the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), as reported by Spotlight in the Daily Maverick.
Eighteen cases are in the Western Cape. Of the 26, 19 are sub-clade Ib. Seven people have been hospitalised and no deaths have been reported this year.
Health department spokesperson Foster Mohale confirmed 3,865 vaccine doses remain, expiring on 31 August 2027. He said buying more doses is under review.
Dr Jacqueline Weyer of the NICD said further cases could not be ruled out while investigations continue.

stories.head: Servier's Becker muscular dystrophy drug fails pivotal trial
stories.stand: The French drugmaker said the GRAND CANYON study missed its main and secondary goals, though the drug's safety profile remained favourable.
stories.say: Servier says its drug sevasemten failed to help people with Becker muscular dystrophy in an 18-month trial, months after it paid 1.55 billion dollars for it.
body: French drugmaker Servier said on Tuesday that sevasemten missed the main goal of a pivotal trial. The drug was being tested in Becker muscular dystrophy, a muscle-wasting disease.

The 18-month, placebo-controlled GRAND CANYON study measured patients' walking and movement ability. It showed no statistically significant benefit, and secondary goals were also missed. Servier said safety and tolerability remained favourable.
Servier said the results did not match some earlier findings, including from a phase 2 study. It will analyse the data further and present full results later.
Endpoints News reports Servier paid $1.55 billion upfront for the drug from Edgewise Therapeutics.

stories.head: UK health agency starts measuring 'forever chemicals' in people's blood
stories.stand: UKHSA says first findings are expected in 2027 and it is not recommending routine PFAS blood tests for individuals.
stories.say: The UK Health Security Agency has begun testing blood and urine samples for PFAS and other chemicals such as lead and arsenic, to set baseline levels for the population.
body: The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has launched a human biomonitoring study to measure chemical levels in the population. It will test blood and urine samples collected through the Health Survey for England.
The study will look for PFAS, often called forever chemicals, as well as lead, arsenic, bisphenols, phthalates and flame retardants. The aim is to set baseline levels to guide future research.
Initial findings are expected in 2027. UKHSA said it is not recommending routine blood testing for PFAS and that people with concerns should contact their GP.
Dr Edward Wynne-Evans of UKHSA said current evidence suggests any health effects are likely to be limited.

stories.head: Brisbane's Mater hospitals to cut about 430 pathology jobs
stories.stand: Staff were told on Monday; Queensland's health minister says Mater has promised no interruption to pathology services for patients.
stories.say: Mater hospitals in Queensland are cutting about 430 pathology jobs and outsourcing the work, saying Medicare funding has not kept pace with costs.
body: Mater is cutting around 430 pathology positions at its hospitals in South Brisbane and Springfield, ABC News reports. Staff were told on Monday.
Pathology work will be outsourced to providers including Sullivan Nicolaides Pathology and Pathology Queensland. More than 100 roles will go within two months and the rest in 2027.
Mater said Medicare funding had not kept pace with rising pathology costs. The union Together Queensland has raised a formal dispute and asked Health Minister Tim Nicholls to intervene.
Mr Nicholls said Mater had assured Queensland Health there would be no interruption to pathology services for patients.

stories.head: Brazil publishes voluntary roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels
stories.stand: The COP30 host released fossil fuel and deforestation roadmaps on Tuesday, ahead of COP31 in Turkey, but campaigners and scientists say they lack timelines.
stories.say: Brazil has published a voluntary roadmap for moving countries away from fossil fuels, days before the COP31 climate talks open in Antalya. Critics say it sets no deadlines.
body: Brazil, which hosted the COP30 climate summit, published a voluntary roadmap on Tuesday setting out how countries can transition away from fossil fuels. A second roadmap covers halting deforestation by 2030.

COP30 president Andre Correa do Lago said Brazil was not suggesting negotiations, and officials described the document as a call to action. Agence Europe reports that 24 countries had signed up before it was finalised, nine of them European.

The COP31 talks open in Antalya, Turkey, on 9 November and run until 20 November. Brazilian officials said the roadmap would be discussed there on 10 November, and the EU has asked for an exchange of views on both roadmaps.

Reaction was mixed. Greenpeace Brazil said the fossil fuel plan sets no clear phase-out targets, while Fanny Petitbon of 350.org called it a useful menu of policy options. Scientist Joeri Rogelj said it lacked timelines and benchmarks.

stories.head: UK climate minister Katie White sets out priorities for COP31
stories.stand: Katie White named electrification, methane cuts and forest protection as UK priorities and said Britain would wait and see on a proposed global electrification goal.
stories.say: UK climate minister Katie White says the science is really scary and should shape the COP31 talks. She named electrification, methane cuts and forests as British priorities.
body: UK climate minister Katie White has said the science on climate change is frightening and must shape the COP31 talks, which open in Antalya, Turkey, next week. She told Carbon Brief the IPCC reports should form the basis of discussions.

White named electrification, methane cuts, forest protection and the transition away from fossil fuels as UK priorities. Turkey's presidency has proposed a voluntary global goal of 35% of final energy coming from electricity by 2035. White said the UK would wait and see.

The UK's new climate finance pledge is £6bn over three years, compared with £11.6bn over the previous five years. White also said the approval of the Jackdaw gas field was in line with the UK's carbon budgets, and reaffirmed the net zero by 2050 target.

stories.head: 2026 on course to tie 2024 as the warmest year on record
stories.stand: A Carbon Brief analysis puts 2026 at about 1.52C above pre-industrial levels, with a record-breaking El Nino expected to push 2027 higher.
stories.say: This year is on course to tie 2024 as the warmest on record, at about 1.52C above pre-industrial levels. A record El Nino means 2027 is expected to be hotter still.
body: This year is very likely to be the warmest or second-warmest on record, according to an analysis by Zeke Hausfather for Carbon Brief published on Tuesday. The best estimate is about 1.52C above pre-industrial levels, essentially level with 2024.
The analysis gives 2026 a 67% chance of beating 2024 in an average of six datasets, and a 93% chance of exceeding 1.5C. August was the warmest August on record in all six datasets.

The current El Nino broke the daily record for a key Pacific temperature index in September. Model forecasts point to a peak near 4C in December. Because global temperatures lag the Pacific, the biggest effect is expected in 2027, which the analysis gives a 96% chance of setting a new record.
Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest winter maximum on 14 September.
