stories.head: US EPA ends 20-year effort to measure air pollution from livestock farms
stories.stand: The agency says data from a 2005-2007 study are too old and limited to use, and it will end a deal that shielded thousands of farms from legal action.
stories.say: The US Environmental Protection Agency has dropped a 20-year effort to estimate air pollution from big livestock farms, saying its data are too old. Critics say farms will escape scrutiny.
body: The US Environmental Protection Agency has abandoned a two-decade effort to develop methods for estimating air pollution from large livestock and poultry operations. It announced the decision on 30 October.

Under a 2005 agreement, about 2,600 animal feeding operations, representing nearly 14,000 farms, were shielded from some legal action in return for joining an industry-funded monitoring study. The EPA says data gathered in 2005-2007 are too old and limited to support reliable methods, and it will end the agreement.

Abigale Tardif, acting head of the EPA's air office, said the agency would rather say so than issue numbers it could not stand behind. The National Pork Producers Council welcomed the move, while Food & Water Watch said it showed no intention of holding the operations to account under the Clean Air Act.
The EPA says the decision does not change how it applies the Clean Air Act. Inside Climate News cites research linking emissions from these operations to nearly 12,700 US deaths a year.

stories.head: South Korea and Turkey sign nuclear financing pact as Seoul eyes Sinop
stories.stand: Korea's Export-Import Bank and Turkey's state nuclear company will study funding options, though Ankara has not yet picked a partner for its Sinop plant.
stories.say: South Korea and Turkey have signed a deal to explore financing for Turkish nuclear projects, as Seoul bids to help build a plant at Sinop on the Black Sea. No partner has been chosen.
body: South Korea's Export-Import Bank and Turkey's state nuclear power company signed a memorandum on Tuesday to explore financing for Turkish nuclear projects. It came during talks in Seoul between Presidents Lee Jae Myung and Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
The deal sets up information exchange and a working group but names no funding amount. It covers projects including Turkey's planned second nuclear plant at Sinop on the Black Sea coast.

Erdogan called South Korea a potential partner for Sinop but did not announce a deal. Ankara says financing and electricity costs will decide its choice. Russia's Rosatom is building Turkey's first plant, at Akkuyu.
The leaders also agreed to expand defence cooperation and signed agreements on energy and mining. It is Erdogan's first visit to South Korea since 2018.

stories.head: Wildfire losses to US buildings could nearly triple by 2060, study finds
stories.stand: University of Colorado Boulder researchers say the biggest rise in risk is in the central US, while the West remains the centre of losses.
stories.say: Wildfire losses to buildings in the US could nearly triple by 2060 without new protections, a study says, with up to 449,100 buildings damaged or destroyed by mid-century.
body: Wildfire losses to buildings in the US could nearly triple by 2060 if nothing changes, according to a study in Nature Communications published on Tuesday. It was led by Virginia Iglesias of the University of Colorado Boulder.
Under a business-as-usual scenario with no new adaptation, the researchers estimate that 133,200 to 449,100 buildings could be damaged or destroyed by mid-century, about 300,000 on average.

The West remains the centre of risk, but the biggest increase is projected in the central US, where grassland fires are rising. In the West, 30% of census tracts with the highest projected risk also face economic hardship.
Max Moritz of UC Santa Barbara, who was not involved, told Inside Climate News that climate models struggle with extreme winds, so some risks may be underestimated.

stories.head: Bolivia declares national emergency as El Nino brings drought and floods
stories.stand: President Rodrigo Paz's decree frees up resources as drought hits tens of thousands of families and communities prepare for possible flooding.
stories.say: Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz has declared a national emergency over El Nino, with drought hitting about 78,000 families and authorities bracing for floods.
body: Bolivia's President Rodrigo Paz declared a nationwide state of emergency on Saturday to free up resources to deal with the effects of El Nino. He warned the weather pattern would hit very hard, with both drought and flooding.

Drought is affecting about 78,000 families, according to officials, and 63 communities have declared drought. Others are preparing for possible floods. A government report says more than 75,000 cattle have died.

The decree covers El Nino risks for 2026-2027 and lets national institutions coordinate with international partners. The World Meteorological Organization puts the chance of El Nino continuing through February 2027 at nearly 100%.

stories.head: Storm Agneta floods eastern Rhodes, sweeping away cars
stories.stand: Hours of heavy rain sent an overflowing river through Archangelos, flooding homes and businesses on the Greek island.
stories.say: Storm Agneta brought flash floods to the Greek island of Rhodes on Monday, with an overflowing river sweeping cars through the village of Archangelos and damaging homes and shops.
body: Storm Agneta brought flash flooding to the Greek island of Rhodes early on Monday. The worst damage was in Archangelos, on the island's east side, where an overflowing river turned roads into torrents.
Floodwaters swept cars along the streets and flooded homes and businesses. Smaller floods hit Afantou and villages in the south. Protothema reported about 17 hours of continuous rain.

Greece's 112 emergency system told residents and visitors on Rhodes to limit their movements. Crews later removed vehicles and cleared drains. Forecasters expected more storms in the Dodecanese before conditions improved.

stories.head: China's 2026 clean tech exports set to avoid as much CO2 as Brazil emits
stories.stand: A CREA analysis says export growth in electric vehicles, wind turbines, batteries and solar is cutting emissions abroad, mostly in the global south.
stories.say: China's exports of solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and electric cars this year could avoid about 450 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, an analysis says.
body: Clean energy technology exported by China this year is on track to avoid about 450 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year once installed, according to the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). That is roughly Brazil's annual emissions.

Over the lifetime of the equipment, the analysis puts avoided emissions at about 8,400 million tonnes, comparable to the yearly emissions of the US and India combined. It was written by CREA analyst Lauri Myllyvirta for Carbon Brief.

In the first nine months of 2026, exports of electric vehicles rose 61% on a year earlier, wind turbines 45%, batteries 39% and solar 22%. About 76% of the lifetime avoided emissions fall in the global south.
Independent experts told Euronews the estimate matched the scale of China's exports but could not validate the data.

stories.head: Vermont signs deal to explore importing Nova Scotia offshore wind power
stories.stand: The agreement could offer New England an alternative to US offshore wind, but there is no clear route yet to carry the power south.
stories.say: Vermont has signed a three-year deal with Nova Scotia to explore importing Canadian offshore wind power, which officials hope could replace US projects facing federal opposition.
body: Vermont has signed a three-year memorandum of understanding with Nova Scotia to explore importing electricity from Canadian offshore wind. Governor Phil Scott and Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston signed the agreement.

Nova Scotia plans about 15 gigawatts of offshore wind. Vermont officials hope the power could replace planned US offshore wind if federal opposition blocks those projects. Massachusetts signed a similar agreement with Nova Scotia earlier this year.
There is no clear path yet to bring the power to the New England grid. Vermont's Highgate link to Canada is outdated, and an upgrade could cost up to about $1 billion.
Vermont PIRG and local renewable developers say the state should instead build more solar and wind within Vermont.

stories.head: Drought leaves Italy's prized white truffles smaller and scarcer
stories.stand: Heat and drought in July and August hurt the Piedmont harvest, with prices at Alba's market about 20 to 30% higher than last year.
stories.say: Summer heat and drought have hit Italy's white truffle harvest around Alba, leaving smaller truffles and pushing prices up by 20 to 30 percent, with Croatia also reporting a poor season.
body: Heat and drought in July and August have hurt this year's white truffle crop in the hills around Alba in Piedmont, according to Antonio Degiacomi, president of Italy's National Centre for Truffle Studies. Dry, compacted soils have produced smaller truffles.

Prices at Alba's truffle market are about 20 to 30% higher than last year, according to the president of the town's International White Truffle Fair. Recent rain has improved conditions and helped larger truffles appear.

In Croatia, a truffle hunter estimated the harvest at about 30% below normal. Communities are planting trees and creating public truffle grounds, but new trees can take more than a decade to host truffles.

stories.head: Binance says $6.3bn hack began with a fake job interview
stories.stand: The exchange says North Korea-linked hackers spent months inside its systems, using malware and an internal AI tool before draining its hot wallets.
stories.say: Binance says the hackers behind its record crypto theft got in through a fake job interview, then used an internal AI tool to reach wallet engineers. It has replaced 98% of the lost assets.
body: Binance says the hackers behind last month's theft of about $6.34bn in crypto first got in through a fake job interview. Binance executive Richard Teng called it a campaign built over many months.

In June, an engineer installed a tampered copy of the Homebrew software tool. Binance removed it, but the attackers had already learned about the engineer and colleagues. In September, a second engineer was approached on a real job platform about a role at a fictitious company. He was told to download a coding task containing malware.

On 20 October the attackers used that machine and an internal AI tool to reach two more engineers' computers. On 29 October they ran a malicious script that gave them access to Binance's wallet signing service. Binance says it cleared the malicious authorisation at 00:10 UTC on 30 October.

Binance says it has replenished 98% of affected assets from its own funds and about $2.85bn has been frozen. The FBI blamed the North Korea-linked group TraderTraitor. On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong said North Korea had no need to talk to the US, calling the accusation part of a hostile policy.

stories.head: Supermarket fridge cyberattacks spread to at least 11 countries
stories.stand: Germany, Romania and the UK reported incidents as the EU called for a collective response; nobody has claimed responsibility.
stories.say: Cyberattacks on supermarket fridges have now hit at least 11 European countries, with Germany, Romania and the UK reporting cases on Tuesday. The EU wants a collective response.
body: Cyberattacks on supermarket fridges and freezers have now hit at least 11 European countries, with Germany, Romania and the UK reporting cases on Tuesday. Stores have thrown away food after units warmed up. Nobody has claimed responsibility.

Italy's government held emergency talks with intelligence chiefs on Tuesday and called the impact highly limited, saying only stores with outdated security were hit. About 20 Italian outlets were affected. Germany reported four stores hit and Romania six.

Britain's National Cyber Security Centre said vulnerable refrigeration technology had been exploited in a small number of UK incidents. Its chief executive, Richard Horne, said it was too early to say who was behind the attacks. The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers said some members were affected.

EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the incidents were not isolated and EU agencies were working on a collective response. Romania's cyber agency director, Dan Cimpean, called the attack semi-amateurish. Belgian federal prosecutors have opened an investigation.

stories.head: German MPs warned their iPhones may have been hit by spyware
stories.stand: Apple alerted members of the Bundestag and government to possible spyware attacks; Germany's cyber agency told them to assume their phones may be compromised.
stories.say: Members of Germany's parliament and government have been warned by Apple that their iPhones may have been targeted by mercenary spyware. Nobody has said who is behind it.
body: Members of the Bundestag and the federal government received Apple alerts warning that their iPhones may have been targeted by mercenary spyware. Digital minister Karsten Wildberger confirmed the warnings on public broadcaster ARD on Sunday.

The alerts began reaching phones on 29 October, according to a letter from Germany's federal cybersecurity office, the BSI. The BSI told recipients to assume their devices may be compromised, because the alerts do not show whether an attack succeeded.

Government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin was taking the warning very seriously. Neither Apple nor German authorities have said who is responsible or how many people were targeted. TechCrunch reported that the latest batch of Apple alerts went to users in 99 countries.

stories.head: Ukrainian and Russian alert apps hacked to send fake nuclear warnings
stories.stand: Ukraine's Air Alert app showed false warnings on Sunday night; hours later Russia said its own emergencies app had been hit by a cyberattack.
stories.say: Ukraine's Air Alert app was hacked on Sunday night to warn of nuclear and chemical threats in Kyiv; hours later, Russia's emergencies app sent false nuclear alerts to 33 regions.
body: Ukraine's public Air Alert app was hacked on Sunday night and briefly warned of nuclear, chemical and street-fighting threats in Kyiv and other areas. The air force said at 11:02pm local time that the alerts were false and there was no radiation threat.

The developers shut the app down, while air raid sirens kept working. The air force said the app is not linked to military command systems. Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications blamed Russia.

About two hours later, Russia's Emergencies Ministry said its own app had suffered a massive cyberattack. False warnings of nuclear warheads reached users in 33 regions, according to Russian state media. The ministry said attackers exploited a weakness in the app's admin panel. It is unclear whether the two attacks are linked.

stories.stand: Google is making its AI tools opt-in for K-12 student accounts, but schools that reject AI entirely must give up Google Search as well.
stories.say: Google will turn off Gemini and Search by default for school-managed student accounts. Schools can keep Search without the Gemini app, but cannot strip out its AI features.
body: Google says Gemini, Gemini in Google Classroom and Google Search will be off by default for school-managed K-12 student accounts. Administrators will have to switch each one on. The New York Times reported the changes are expected in early 2027.
Schools can turn off Gemini and keep Search. But they cannot disable only AI Overviews or AI Mode, so schools that exclude AI entirely also lose Search.

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google was using its monopoly power to force AI on public schools. Google said the change expands schools' options and answers educators' requests for finer control over student AI use.

stories.head: EU court adviser says Gemini answers can breach publishers' rights
stories.stand: Advocate General Maciej Szpunar gave a non-binding opinion in a Hungarian publisher's case against Google, the first EU court case on chatbots and press content.
stories.say: An adviser to the EU's top court says AI chatbots like Google's Gemini can infringe press publishers' rights in some cases, such as getting round paywalls. The opinion is not binding.
body: An adviser to the EU's top court says chatbots that reuse press articles to answer users can infringe publishers' rights in certain circumstances. Advocate General Maciej Szpunar gave his opinion on Tuesday in a case brought by Hungarian publisher Like Company against Google's Gemini.

He said infringement could arise if a chatbot reached an article by getting round paywalls or other barriers. Recognisably reproducing an article's wording could also infringe. Facts in news reports are not protected, he said.

Szpunar advised the court not to rule on questions about training AI models. He said such use is generally permitted under an EU data mining exception. Google said Gemini creates original outputs and offers publishers opt-out controls.
The opinion is not binding. The court usually follows its advisers and is expected to rule in the coming months.

stories.head: Anthropic says AI may soon sharply speed up its own development
stories.stand: In an amended filing ahead of its planned stock market listing, the Claude maker warns progress could outpace its safety measures.
stories.say: Anthropic has told US regulators it may imminently reach its own threshold for dramatically accelerated, AI-driven progress, though no current model has crossed it.
body: Anthropic says its internal estimates for future models suggest it may imminently meet its own definition of dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI. The warning is in an amended S-1 filing to the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 2 November, ahead of a planned public offering.

The company says no current model has been designated as crossing that threshold and it is still assessing the data. It admits it has previously failed to spot significant accelerations until after they happened.

Anthropic says Claude wrote over 90% of contributions to its codebase in September. It does not expect to let Claude fully design and build new frontier models without meaningful human supervision. It is considering changes to keep humans in control.
The filing also says the company's safeguards are incomplete. Some commentators said such claims in an IPO filing may also serve as marketing.

stories.head: New York Times sues Brave over alleged scraping for AI firms
stories.stand: The Times and three other newspapers allege the browser maker scraped their articles and supplied them to AI companies; Brave did not immediately comment.
stories.say: The New York Times has sued the privacy browser Brave, accusing it of scraping articles and passing them to AI companies. Three other US newspapers filed a similar suit.
body: The New York Times sued browser maker Brave in federal court in Manhattan on Monday. The Daily News, the Chicago Tribune and the Orlando Sentinel filed a similar lawsuit the same day.

The suits allege Brave scraped the papers' content and passed it to AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI and Cohere. They say Brave built an index of more than 30 billion web pages with a crawler publishers could not block.

The Times also targets a Brave feature that gets round paywalls, and Brave's blocking of publishers' ads while selling its own. It seeks an injunction and damages. Brave did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

stories.head: Canva to cut or move 1,271 jobs as growth slows
stories.stand: The Australian design company says 22% of its staff will be cut, given new roles or relocated in a restructure its founder calls a refounding.
stories.say: Australian design firm Canva says 1,271 roles, 22% of its staff, will be cut, changed or relocated after growth slowed for the first time in a decade and AI costs rose.
body: Canva says 1,271 roles, about 22% of its workforce, will be cut, changed or relocated in its first major job cuts. Founder and chief executive Melanie Perkins said the aim was to refound the company.

Perkins said growth slowed this year for the first time in a decade. Rising costs of serving AI to mostly non-paying users delayed some product rollouts, and backers have marked down the company's value.

Product, growth and platform teams will merge into one organisation, with Sydney as the main product base. From January most hybrid staff must be in the office two to three days a week. Departing staff will get at least six months' salary.

stories.head: AMD posts record $13.4bn quarter as data centre sales nearly double
stories.stand: The chipmaker forecast about $17bn in fourth-quarter revenue and booked a $1,097m charge on warrants issued to customers.
stories.say: Chipmaker AMD has reported record quarterly revenue of $13.4bn, up 45%, with data centre sales up 97%. It expects about $17bn in the final quarter of the year.
body: AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of $13.4bn on Tuesday, up 45% from a year earlier. Its data centre business grew 97% to a record $8.5bn.
Gaming revenue fell 40% to $773m, while client chip sales rose 7%. Net profit was $2.4bn under standard accounting.

AMD booked a $1,097m charge for the changing value of warrants issued to certain customers, which it does not name. Chief executive Lisa Su said growth should accelerate further, with fourth-quarter revenue forecast at about $17bn.

stories.head: Apple starts testing conversation recaps on Apple Watch
stories.stand: Features that rewind and summarise conversations are in developer beta for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, with a public beta to follow.
stories.say: Apple has begun beta testing Audio Intelligence for the Apple Watch, which can show the last 15 seconds of speech as text and summarise conversations into notes.
body: Apple's Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch have entered developer beta testing with the iOS 27.3 update. A public beta will follow, but Apple has given no release date. The features work on Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

Live Rewind shows the last 15 seconds of speech as text on the watch. Siri Recaps creates short conversation notes; Apple says it does not save raw audio, identify speakers or produce word-for-word transcripts.

Users review recaps daily and choose which to keep. Unsaved recaps are deleted after seven days. Apple says audio is processed on the paired iPhone and its Private Cloud Compute, with recaps deleted from the cloud immediately afterwards.

stories.head: Ukrainian start-up's pocket receiver taps Russian drone video
stories.stand: Kyiv firm CODE380's D-Vision SDR picks up unencrypted video feeds from many Russian drones, though experts warn against relying on such detectors.
stories.say: A Kyiv start-up has built a pocket-sized receiver that picks up live video from many Russian drones, letting soldiers see where a drone is heading before it strikes.
body: Kyiv equipment start-up CODE380 has developed the D-Vision SDR, a pocket-sized receiver that shows live camera video from many Russian drones. Operators can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before impact.

It works because those drones send video over the air without encryption. The device also listens on radio channels that Russia's newer Molniya drones began using for video in June. It weighs about 10 ounces, less than half the weight of rival Ukrainian models.

Serhii Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine's president, has warned that relying too heavily on detectors could be fatal. He also said a switch to digital video could blind such receivers.

stories.head: Spanish writer Cristina Fernández Cubas wins the Cervantes Prize
stories.stand: The jury said the Catalan-born author renewed the short story and transformed fantasy writing in Spanish.
stories.say: Spanish writer Cristina Fernández Cubas has won the Cervantes Prize, the top award for Spanish-language literature, worth 125,000 euros. She is the seventh woman to win it.
body: Spain's culture minister, Ernest Urtasun, announced on Tuesday that Cristina Fernández Cubas has won the 2026 Cervantes Prize. The award carries 125,000 euros.

Fernández Cubas was born in 1945 in Arenys de Mar, near Barcelona. She worked as a journalist before turning to fiction, and is best known for short-story collections such as Mi hermana Elba and La habitación de Nona.
The jury praised her originality and consistency, saying she renewed the contemporary short story and transformed fantasy literature in Spanish.
According to elDiario.es, she is the seventh woman to win the prize since it was created in 1976. Mexican writer Gonzalo Celorio won in 2025. The prize is traditionally presented on 23 April.

stories.head: Philippe Jaenada wins France's Prix Goncourt
stories.stand: The 62-year-old won France's top literary prize for a book investigating an unsolved killing of a young woman in Paris.
stories.say: Philippe Jaenada has won France's Prix Goncourt for a novel reopening an old Paris murder case. As tradition dictates, the 62-year-old gets a cheque for just 10 euros.
body: French writer Philippe Jaenada won the 2026 Prix Goncourt on Tuesday for L'Inconnue du quai de Javel. The jury announced its choice at the Drouant restaurant in Paris.
The 62-year-old's book revisits the unsolved killing of a young woman found by the Seine, drawing on old police files. It is published by Flammarion.
He beat three other finalists: Yannick Haenel, Clémentine Mélois and Sylvain Prudhomme. By tradition the winner receives a symbolic cheque for 10 euros.

Euronews reported that a Lyon bookseller criticised the shortlist because all four books came from publishers in the Madrigall group. The Renaudot prize went to François-Henri Désérable for Le Palais.

stories.head: Collins Dictionary names 'mogging' its word of the year
stories.stand: The slang term, which began in online bodybuilding and 'manosphere' circles, means to outshine or upstage someone.
stories.say: Collins Dictionary has picked mogging, meaning to outshine or upstage someone, as its word of the year. Collins says use of the slang term rose 210 per cent in a year.
body: Collins Dictionary named 'mogging' its 2026 word of the year on Tuesday. The word means to outshine, outperform or overshadow someone or something.
Collins said use of the term rose by 210 per cent over the year. Its lexicographers track a corpus of about 27 billion words, including social media.
According to a Collins blog post cited by ABC News, the word began around 2016 in bodybuilding culture and spread through the online 'manosphere' before going mainstream.
Other shortlisted words included carspreading, ghost job, bixie, hydration break, Manchesterism and P(doom). Dictionary.com chose 'maxxing' as its word for 2026.

body: Australian author Craig Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail on Monday for distributing and possessing child exploitation material, ABC News reported.
Judge Hayley Cormann handed down the sentence in the WA District Court. Silvey had pleaded guilty to the two charges earlier in 2026.

Silvey's 2009 novel Jasper Jones sold more than 600,000 copies worldwide and was made into a feature film.

stories.head: Elizabeth Holmes documentary tops the US box office
stories.stand: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's film beat Clayface to first place, a rare feat for a documentary.
stories.say: A24's documentary You Can See Everything, about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has topped the US box office, edging out Clayface in its third weekend.
body: You Can See Everything, a documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, was the top film in US cinemas over the Halloween weekend.
The A24 release, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, was in its third weekend and has taken about $64 million in total. Clayface came second with $10.4 million.
Rotten Tomatoes said it was the first non-concert documentary to lead the box office since Fahrenheit 9/11 in June 2004.
The film opened to just over $15 million, according to The A.V. Club, and then expanded to more than 3,000 cinemas.

body: La bola negra had taken 36.7 million euros at Spanish cinemas by 1 November, from 5.4 million cinema-goers, according to Euronews.

stories.head: Detroit techno pioneer Juan Atkins dies aged 64
stories.stand: The DJ and producer, behind Cybotron and Model 500, was found unresponsive in a hotel room before a show in Mexico City.
stories.say: Juan Atkins, one of the founders of Detroit techno, has died at 64. He was found unresponsive in a Mexico City hotel room before a show, his agency said.
body: Juan Atkins, a founding figure of Detroit techno, has died aged 64. His management agency confirmed the death on Sunday.
According to NME and Hot Press, he was found unresponsive in a hotel room ahead of a show in Mexico City and taken to hospital. No cause of death has been given.
Born in Detroit in 1962, Atkins formed the Belleville Three with Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. With Richard Davis he formed Cybotron, whose track Clear was later sampled by Missy Elliott.
He also recorded as Model 500 and founded the Metroplex label. Kevin Saunderson and Detroit mayor Mary Sheffield were among those paying tribute.

body: Steve Ellis, the singer with 1960s pop group Love Affair, has died aged 76. A statement on his official Facebook page said he died on the evening of 30 October from complications of a chronic illness.
Love Affair's version of Everlasting Love reached number one on the UK singles chart. The band also had hits with Rainbow Valley and A Day Without Love.
Ellis joined the band, then called the Soul Survivors, as a teenager. He left in 1969 to go solo and later led his own touring version of Love Affair.
Paul Weller was among those paying tribute, describing Ellis as a close friend, Hello! reported.

body: Queens of the Stone Age have announced nine European concerts for June 2027, NME reported. The run starts in Hannover on 13 June and ends at the Pula Arena in Croatia on 30 June.

The tour follows the band's ninth album, Perfecth, released on 30 October on Matador Records. North American shows are planned for May 2027.
No UK dates had been announced, though NME said they were expected in the coming weeks.

stories.head: Grand Egyptian Museum marks first year with new light show
stories.stand: The museum near the Giza pyramids says it had more than 5 million visitors in its first year and is raising ticket prices.
stories.say: Egypt's Grand Egyptian Museum has marked its first year with Eternal Sun, a 35-minute light show in its Grand Hall. Its chief executive says it drew more than 5 million visitors.
body: The Grand Egyptian Museum in Giza launched a light-and-sound show called Eternal Sun on Sunday to mark one year since its opening.
The 35-minute show turns the museum's Grand Hall into a stage, using projection, lighting and live music in Arabic and English. It will run for six months, until 30 April 2027.

Chief executive Ahmed Ghoneim said the museum received more than 5 million visitors in its first year. Arab News reported that admission prices are rising by 20 Egyptian pounds for Egyptian adults and $5 for foreign adults.
The museum displays the treasures of Tutankhamun, whose tomb was found by Howard Carter's team in 1922.

stories.head: Satellite radar reveals buried ancient complex in Egypt's Nile Delta
stories.stand: A team spotted the structure with European radar satellites, then confirmed its walls by digging six to seven metres down.
stories.say: Researchers using satellite radar have found a large mudbrick complex, about 2,600 years old, buried under the ancient city of Buto in Egypt's Nile Delta.
body: Egyptian researchers have found a large buried mudbrick complex at Buto, also known as Tell el-Fara'in, in the Nile Delta, Live Science and Gizmodo reported.
The team first spotted an oval anomaly about 128 metres by 62 metres in radar images from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites. Ground surveys then mapped the layers below.
An excavation 6 to 7 metres deep confirmed mudbrick walls resting on a layer of sand, along with religious objects. The complex is thought to be about 2,600 years old.
Its purpose is unclear. Gizmodo said it could be a temple, a religious service complex, a priests' residence or a funerary building. The study appears in the journal Acta Geophysica.

stories.head: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel dies after on-pitch collision
stories.stand: The 30-year-old died in hospital on Tuesday morning after being struck in the chest during a Spanish second-division match on Monday.
stories.say: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel has died aged 30, a day after colliding with Andorra's goalkeeper; Spanish authorities are investigating and Tuesday's domestic fixtures were postponed.
body: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel died on Tuesday morning, aged 30, the club said. He had collided with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono in a second-division match on Monday.
Owono's knee appeared to strike him in the chest as the goalkeeper rushed out for a long ball. Owono was shown a straight red card and the match, level at 2-2, was abandoned.
De Miguel was treated on the pitch and taken to hospital in Santa Cruz, where he died. Spanish authorities have opened an investigation; local media say a police homicide unit is involved.

The Spanish Football Federation postponed all Tuesday fixtures, including Copa del Rey ties. Moments of silence were held before Champions League matches, and tributes came from Real Madrid, Barcelona and FC Andorra.

stories.head: Barcelona beat Aston Villa 3-0 to end Villa's perfect start
stories.stand: Yamal opened the scoring after seven minutes and Raphinha scored twice in the second half at Camp Nou.
stories.say: Lamine Yamal scored early and Raphinha added two after the break as Barcelona beat Aston Villa 3-0 on Tuesday, ending Villa's perfect start in the Champions League.
body: Barcelona beat Aston Villa 3-0 at Camp Nou on Tuesday in the fourth round of Champions League league-phase matches.
Lamine Yamal scored after seven minutes when Villa lost the ball in their own box. UEFA said the goal made him the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history.
Raphinha scored twice in the second half, the second from a Joao Cancelo cross. Barcelona kept their first Champions League clean sheet in 19 games, Al Jazeera reported.
Villa's club-record run of four straight Champions League wins ended. Both sides now have nine points. The Champions League anthem was not played before kick-off, in tribute to Jesus de Miguel.

stories.say: Manchester United came from two goals down to beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford on Tuesday, with Matheus Cunha scoring twice late on, ending a nine-match winless run under Michael Carrick.
body: Manchester United beat Roma 3-2 at Old Trafford on Tuesday after trailing 2-0. Matias Soule and Donyell Malen, from a penalty, scored for Roma early in the first half.
Bruno Fernandes scored a retaken penalty after his first attempt was saved and Roma players were found to have entered the box early. Matheus Cunha then scored twice in the closing stages.
Cunha was sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card. Carlos Baleba went off injured early in the second half.
The victory ended a nine-match winless run. ESPN said it boosted Michael Carrick's hopes of keeping his job, with United at home to Aston Villa on Sunday.

stories.stand: The relegated club dismissed Nuno on Tuesday after back-to-back defeats left them eighth in the Championship.
stories.say: West Ham have sacked Nuno Espirito Santo with the club eighth in the Championship, six points off the top; former midfielder Scott Parker is reported to be lined up as his successor.
body: West Ham sacked head coach Nuno Espirito Santo on Tuesday, 13 games into their Championship season. The club said the board felt a change was necessary.
West Ham are eighth, six points behind leaders Middlesbrough, after defeats by Southampton and West Brom. Nuno arrived in September 2025 but could not keep the club in the Premier League.
Assistant Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left. Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will prepare the team for Wednesday's match against Cardiff City.
Scott Parker, a former West Ham player, is reported to be lined up as the next head coach. The club has not confirmed an appointment.

stories.head: Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia pushed back by almost a year
stories.stand: The Asian Football Confederation moved the 24-team tournament to December 2027 to January 2028, citing travel disruption from the regional conflict.
stories.say: The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia has been rescheduled to run from the twenty-third of December 2027, nearly a year later than planned, because of the regional conflict.
body: The Asian Football Confederation said on Tuesday that the 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia will now run from 23 December 2027 to 21 January 2028.
The 24-team tournament had been due to start in Riyadh on 7 January 2027. The AFC cited logistical complexities and travel disruption linked to the regional conflict.
Al Jazeera reported that Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks since September. The AFC will submit the new dates to Fifa for approval.

body: Haas said on Tuesday that Esteban Ocon will not return to a race seat this season. Team principal Ayao Komatsu said discussions with the driver would remain internal.
Ocon was replaced mid-weekend at the Mexico City Grand Prix by reserve Ryo Hirakawa, after a reported confrontation with Komatsu. Ocon denies the row turned physical.
Rafael Camara, 21, the Formula 2 championship leader and a Ferrari academy driver, will make his debut at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix alongside Ollie Bearman.
Haas and Ocon had already agreed to part at the end of the season. Haas has not said who will drive in the remaining rounds.

body: Jodie Burrage, 27, lost 3-6, 6-3, 7-5 to India's Vaishnavi Adkar in the first round of the Chennai Open. It was her first WTA singles main-draw match in 16 months.

Burrage, ranked 474th, had last played a tour main-draw match at Wimbledon in July 2025. A joint WTA and ITF report found 458 players were targeted by abuse in 2024.

body: Alex Mitchell will miss all of England's Nations Championship campaign after a scan on Monday confirmed a hamstring injury. It is his fourth hamstring injury this year.
The 29-year-old Northampton scrum-half, who has 32 caps, was hurt against Gloucester. He misses Tests against Australia, Japan and New Zealand and the finals weekend.
Jack van Poortvliet is expected to start against Australia on Sunday. Ben Spencer and Harry Randall have been called into Steve Borthwick's 36-man squad.
Fin Smith, Mitchell's Northampton teammate, is racing to be fit for Sunday after a calf problem.
